1.pericope_label: Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may have free course, and be glorified, even as it is with you: And that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith. But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil. And we have confidence in the Lord touching you, that ye both do and will do the things which we command you. And the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God, and into the patient waiting for Christ.

schools.summary: Calvin insists the request is not personal: Paul, who surpassed others in prayer, still wanted theirs, and wanted it for the gospel’s advance and the Church’s welfare rather than his own safety. He separates the two verbs, the first meaning dissemination and the second the power to renew men, so that Christian holiness is what glorifies the word. On the opponents he names Chrysostom as confining them to false teachers and deliberately extends the term to every kind of danger, noting Paul’s journey toward Jerusalem under a standing forewarning. Gill identifies the section’s subject as discipline, itemises what a congregation should ask for its ministers, and reads the Lord’s faithfulness as comfort against the discouragement of the verse before.

Henry turns the request into a doctrine of fellowship. Praying for one another in absence is one of the ways the communion of saints is maintained, so that men separated by distance meet at the throne of grace, and those who can do or receive no other kindness may do and receive a very great one; from which he draws the duty of praying for ministers generally and not only for one’s own.

Ellicott renders the opening formula as for the rest, quotes Chrysostom on the mutuality of the request, and takes the petition for the word literally as may run along, hearing speed and security in it; on the disputed adjective he pushes hardest, from misplaced to extravagant and monstrous, illustrating from the dying thief. Barnes traces the same word through its uses and concludes it indicates misplacement rather than malice. Robertson notes that the two verbs of the petition are joined nowhere else in the New Testament, traces the figure to the stadium, relays Lightfoot’s triumphant career, and lists the adjective’s full range without choosing.

Clarke denies that the opening word means finally at all, reads the disputed adjective as disorderly and unmanageable rather than monstrous, and makes the sharpest lexical claim in the passage: that the faith not all men have is fidelity rather than belief, proved by the wordplay with the Lord’s faithfulness in the next verse. He also allows that the evil they are kept from may be read as the evil one. Wesley glosses the running of the word as going on swiftly without interruption and being owned as divine, and takes those without faith to be more or less unreasonable and wicked.

Chrysostom states the balance the passage depends on: having committed everything to the prayers of the saints we must not be idle, nor when working good despise that help, since prayer effects great things but only where we also work. He reads the promise to stablish and guard as immediately qualified by the confidence that they will obey, lest they think the whole of God and fall asleep; God promised to save and will save, but as he promised, to those willing to hear and not like stocks and stones.

debates: What the opening word means, and whether finally is a fair rendering.
Whether the disputed adjective indicates misplacement, indiscipline, or monstrousness.
Who the unreasonable men are: unbelieving Jews, false teachers within the Church, or every kind of enemy.
Whether the faith that not all men have is belief or trustworthiness.
Whether the evil they are kept from is a thing or a person.
outliers: Calvin names Chrysostom’s narrower identification of the opponents and deliberately widens it.
Ellicott quotes Chrysostom twice on the request for prayer, and Chrysostom is himself a witness in this chapter.
Clarke rests a lexical argument on the wordplay between the men who lack faith and the Lord who is faithful.
Robertson observes that the two verbs of the petition occur together nowhere else in the New Testament.
Barnes reads the adjective as indicating disorder rather than malice, against Ellicott’s monstrous.
Henry makes intercession in absence a means of grace for those who can render no other kindness.
themes: Finally, brethren, pray for us
That the word may run and be glorified
Unreasonable and wicked men
All men have not faith
But the Lord is faithful
The patient waiting for Christ

6.pericope_label: Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us. For yourselves know how ye ought to follow us: for we behaved not ourselves disorderly among you; Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you: Not because we have not power, but to make ourselves an ensample unto you to follow us. For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes the power of judgment, which he places in the whole church, from the executive power of admission and exclusion, which he places in the elders. On the waiver of maintenance he is alert to the consequences for other men: Paul kept the right alive while declining to use it, lest ministers who could not support themselves be injured by the precedent and lest covetous hearers turn it against ministerial maintenance altogether. Calvin argues that disorderly here means idle rather than scandalous, since the word is not applied to dissolute men but to those in no useful occupation, and describes the offenders as inquisitive drifters living at others’ expense; he calls Paul’s moderation singular and contrasts it with men who abuse authority to the injury of their brethren.

Henry states the principle the section rests on: the best Christian society will contain faulty persons, perfection not being available on this side heaven, and it is precisely bad conduct that produces good rules — the disorders at Thessalonica having yielded laws of permanent use.

Barnes traces the escalation from exhortation in the earlier letter to command here, admits that the original cause of the idleness is unknown, and limits the maxim’s force to support at the public expense while noting its currency among Jews and Greeks alike. Ellicott takes acting in the Lord’s name literally, as naming the name in the act, and reads the demand for imitation as implying both precept and example, expressly against Chrysostom’s reading of example alone; he also observes how carefully Paul defends the apostolate’s rights for others rather than himself. Robertson takes the name as authority instead, glosses the military metaphor behind disorderly, calls the call to imitation daring, and notes that Paul accepted help where it could not be misread.

Clarke reads the disorderly as men out of their rank who submit to no discipline, and takes the tradition emphatically as the written orders of the first epistle, denying that any unwritten or uncertain saying is meant. He prefers right to power, and on the maxim about working holds it a proverb among the Jews that universal nature teaches, founded on the sentence passed in Eden, with the corollary that it is a sin to relieve merely artificial necessities. Wesley narrows disorderly to the failure to work, and against Clarke takes the tradition to cover the spoken admonition as well as the written one.

Chrysostom appears here only as the reading Ellicott argues against: he made the tradition the Thessalonians had received consist of the apostles’ example without any accompanying precept, which would simplify the logic of the sentence but leaves out the rule they were also given.

debates: What walking disorderly means: scandalous living, indiscipline, or idleness.
Whether the tradition departed from is the written epistle only or the spoken admonition as well.
Whether acting in the name of the Lord means by his authority or with his name pronounced.
Whether the tradition consisted of precept, example, or both.
Who in the church holds the power to exclude.
outliers: Gill separates the power of judgment from the power of execution and assigns them to different parties.
Clarke uses the word tradition to deny that anything unwritten is in view, and Wesley reads it to include the spoken word.
Ellicott names Chrysostom’s reading of the tradition as example without precept and rejects it.
Calvin compares the idle to drones that make no honey and live on the honey of others.
Barnes admits that what first made the Thessalonians idle is not known.
Clarke draws from the maxim that relieving artificial necessities is itself a sin.
themes: Withdraw from every brother that walketh disorderly
Not after the tradition received of us
We behaved not ourselves disorderly
Wrought with labour and travail night and day
Not because we have not power
If any would not work, neither should he eat

11.pericope_label: For we hear that there are some which walk among you disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies. Now them that are such we command and exhort by our Lord Jesus Christ, that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread. But ye, brethren, be not weary in well doing. And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed. Yet count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

schools.summary: Calvin treats these idlers as the seed of monasticism, tracing a line from men who made free with others’ tables under a pretext of religion to the idle monks Augustine wrote a book against, whose pride lay in claiming exemption from labour. He argues that the most peaceable men are those occupied in a lawful calling, and grounds the severity of the sentence on the fact that refusing this command is rebellion against God rather than against a man; he expects the offender to be reported to Paul first and excommunicated afterwards, so that shame may work repentance. Gill explains how a man with the care of all the churches kept informed, and is careful that the charge should not touch the innocent.

Barnes leaves open how the report reached Paul, explains the drift into meddling by the emptiness of an idle life, and makes the freshest observation in the section: that the undeserving discourage charity toward the deserving until a giver, unable to discriminate, refuses everyone. He keeps the construction that makes this epistle the thing disobeyed, and reads the closing caution as the governing principle of all discipline, since the standing danger is to treat a brother as an adversary. Ellicott supposes the bearers of the first letter brought the news, hears aimlessness in the phrase among you, notes the scornful wordplay, counts the severe verb’s fourth appearance and the entreaty that follows it, and argues that eating one’s own bread would not exclude a common purse. Robertson credits Ellicott’s rendering of the pun, calls the offenders theological dead-beats, and glosses the marking from commercial usage as putting a tag on a man.

Clarke supplies the fiercest description of the busybodies as newsmongers and telltales, a curse to the neighbourhood, and answers with a phrase: less noise and more work. He reports the alternative construction of the sentence about the epistle without adopting it, and reverses the final caution to good effect, urging that such a man be counted more an enemy to himself than to the church, and his soul laboured for. Wesley reduces the positive command to letting other people’s concerns alone, and draws the negative boundary precisely: no intimacy, no familiarity, no needless correspondence.

debates: Whether by this epistle attaches to the disobedience or to the marking of the offender.
How the report of the disorder reached Paul.
Whether eating one’s own bread rules out a common purse.
What limit the closing caution sets on the discipline just commanded.
Whether the offender was to be reported to Paul before being excluded.
outliers: Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson independently notice the wordplay between working and being busy.
Robertson adopts Ellicott’s rendering of that pun in preference to his own.
Calvin reads the passage as the earliest evidence against monastic idleness and cites a treatise of Augustine’s to that effect.
Barnes warns that the undeserving harden givers against the deserving, so that discrimination fails and charity stops altogether.
Ellicott raises, without settling, whether the phrase is compatible with community of goods.
Robertson explains the command to note the man from the language of receipts and formal notices.
themes: Working not at all, but busybodies
With quietness they work
Eat their own bread
Be not weary in well doing
Note that man, and have no company with him
Admonish him as a brother

16.pericope_label: Now the Lord of peace himself give you peace always by all means. The Lord be with you all. The salutation of Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle: so I write. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

schools.summary: Calvin refuses to read the prayer as a detached formula. It follows directly on the order to admonish rather than to hate, and states as prayer what could have been stated as command, since concord is God’s work; he notes that a prayer of this kind still carries the force of a precept, and suspects a second petition inside it, that the unruly be restrained from troubling the church. Gill identifies the Lord of peace as the author of peace in his churches, who both calls for it and encourages it, and describes the division of labour by which the letter was written and then signed.

Henry itemises the peace prayed for — with God, in their own consciences, among themselves, and with all men — and asked for always and in everything. He takes by all means as by every method, arguing that a people possessing the means of grace should use every means of peace as well, since peace is as difficult as it is desirable.

Ellicott connects the prayer to the discipline through Chrysostom’s observation about quarrels, extends by all means across every subject the letter has raised, and draws the sharpest distinction of the three: the token is the autograph addition itself rather than its wording, the salutation proper begins only at the benediction, and this verse exists to point at that one. He also confronts the audacity of forging an apostolic letter and explains it by the first epistle’s not yet having acquired its later standing. Robertson notes the change from the God of peace to the Lord of peace, takes the latter of Christ, and treats the signature as each church’s means of authenticating a letter in a period that already had forgeries. Barnes reads the token as a known mark or manner of signing.

Clarke names the Lord of peace from the prophet as the Prince of peace and the fountain from which it comes, and reports a textual variant of some weight: a number of manuscripts, versions and fathers read in every place rather than in every way, which turns the petition into a prayer for prosperity always and everywhere. On the signature he explains the amanuensis practice and observes that such a safeguard would be necessary precisely because forged letters were in circulation.

Chrysostom is present here only as Ellicott reports him, suggesting that the prayer for peace answers a real risk: that administering the discipline just commanded would itself set quarrels going in the congregation.

debates: Whether the prayer for peace is a closing formula or an answer to the discipline just commanded.
Whether by all means describes every method of peace or every form of it.
Whether the text reads in every way or in every place.
What exactly the token is: the autograph words, the act of signing, or a known manner of signature.
Where the salutation proper begins.
outliers: Calvin holds that a prayer of this kind carries the force of a command.
Ellicott reports Chrysostom’s suggestion that the discipline itself threatened the church’s peace.
Clarke preserves a variant reading supported by manuscripts, versions and fathers alike.
Ellicott argues that this verse is a pointer to the next rather than the salutation itself.
Robertson ends on the wish that the autograph copy might one day be found.
Ellicott explains the plausibility of forgery by the first epistle’s not yet having its later authority.
themes: The Lord of peace himself give you peace
Always by all means
The Lord be with you all
The salutation of Paul with mine own hand
The token in every epistle
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ
